title: Why people steal
translation: Even people who seem to have no feelings come out with something good now and then. A fierce-looking warrior from the east once asked the man next to him, "Do you have children?"
"Then you don't know what it is to feel for things. You must have a cold heart, and that frightens me. It's children that teach you to feel everything."

He was right. Without the love between parents and children, would a man like that have any compassion in him? Even people who never cared about their parents find out what their parents felt once they have children of their own.

Someone who has left the world and owns nothing at all sees people tied down by their families, sees them flattering everyone and always wanting more, and looks down on them. That's wrong. Put yourself in their place. For parents, a wife and children you really love, you'd forget all shame. You might even steal.

So instead of tying up thieves and punishing nothing but the crime, run the world so that people don't go hungry and cold. "Without a steady living, people have no steady heart." People steal when they're desperate. As long as the country is badly run and people freeze and starve, there will be no end of criminals. Making people suffer, driving them to break the law and then punishing them for it is a cruel thing to do.

How do you help them, then? If those at the top stop spending on luxuries, look after the people and encourage farming, the people below will be better off. There's no doubt about it. If someone has food and clothes like anyone else and still does wrong, that's the one you can call a real thief.

literal: Even people who seem heartless say a good word.
A certain fearsome-looking eastern warrior, meeting the person beside him, asked 'Do you have children?', and when he answered 'I have not even one',

(the warrior) said, 'Then you will not know the feeling of things. I am very afraid that you must have an unfeeling heart. It is through children that one comes to know all feelings': that is surely right.
If not for the way of love (between kin), would there be compassion in the heart of such a person?
Even those without filial devotion come to know their parents' feelings only when they have children.
That a person who has abandoned the world and has nothing at all, seeing that people with many ties generally flatter in everything and have deep desires, despises them utterly, is wrong.
If one thinks putting oneself in that person's heart, for truly beloved parents, wife and children, one would forget shame and might even steal.
So, rather than binding thieves and punishing only wrongdoing, one would like to govern the world so that its people do not starve or freeze.
When people have no constant livelihood, they have no constant heart.
People steal when they are at the end of their resources.
If the world is not governed and there is the suffering of freezing and starving, criminals will not cease.
To make people suffer, make them break the law, and then punish them for it is a pitiful thing.
Now, if one asks how one should benefit people: if those above stop their luxury and waste, care for the people and encourage farming, there can be no doubt that there will be profit for those below.
Someone who, with food and clothing as ordinary in the world, still does wrong: that one should call a true thief.

notes.quote: ある荒夷の恐ろしげなるが
notes.text: {荒夷|あらえびす}: 'rough barbarian', the capital's word for a warrior from the eastern provinces (the 1925 edition: 'a rough country warrior from the east'). の … が: 'a certain eastern warrior, a fearsome-looking one'. {傍|かたへ}: the person next to him.

notes.quote: 物のあはれは知り給はじ
notes.text: {物|もの}のあはれ: the feeling that things stir in you (the 1925 edition: 'the fine points of human feeling'). More than four hundred years later, Motoori Norinaga made 'knowing the feeling of things' the heart of his reading of Japanese literature. Here a rough warrior uses the phrase, and Kenkō agrees with him.

notes.quote: 子故にこそ、万の哀れは思ひ知らるれ
notes.text: こそ … るれ: the realis form of る, 'one comes to know'. あはれ again: it is the word of the whole section.

{恩愛|おんあい}: a Buddhist term for the love between parents and children, and husband and wife. Buddhism usually counts it as a tie that holds you back; here it is the thing that teaches compassion ({慈悲|じひ}).
{孝養|けうやう}: devotion to your parents, a central virtue in Confucian teaching.

notes.quote: よろづにするすみなるが
notes.text: するすみ: 'owning nothing at all, with empty hands' (the 1925 edition). ほだし: 'fetters', the family ties that keep someone in the world. Kenkō had himself left the world, so he is describing his own kind.

notes.quote: かなしからむ親のため妻子のためには
notes.text: かなし here is 'dearly loved' (the 1925 edition), not modern 'sad'. A false friend that comes up again and again in classical Japanese.

notes.quote: 人恒の産なき時は恒の心なし
notes.text: From the Chinese philosopher Mencius: without a steady way to make a living ({恒産|こうさん}), ordinary people have no steady heart ({恒心|こうしん}), and they will do anything. The 1925 edition quotes the Chinese text. The saying is still current in Japanese as {恒産|こうさん}なき{者|もの}は{恒心|こうしん}なし.
{不便|ふびん}: 'pitiful, cruel', not modern {不便|ふべん} 'inconvenient' (see section 128).

notes.quote: まことの盗人とはいふべき
notes.text: ぞ … べき: ぞ needs the attributive form. The section began with a warrior's remark about children and ends with a programme for government.
